title: Reading files, EOF and stream error indicators
learningObjectives: Explain the C concept and its rules.
Trace the example and describe data flow.
Identify relevant failure and boundary cases.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: Input functions such as fgetc return an int so they can represent every unsigned-char value plus the distinct EOF indicator. feof reports whether end-of-file has been encountered; ferror reports whether a stream error occurred. EOF is usually detected after a read attempt fails to produce another character.
understand.whyItMatters: Correct read loops distinguish normal end-of-file from an I/O error and avoid storing EOF in a char before checking it.
understand.analogy: Treat the operation as a clearly specified contract between the program and its data.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's type, lifetime, I/O and object representation rules.

explain.narrative:
Input functions such as fgetc return an int so they can represent every unsigned-char value plus the distinct EOF indicator. feof reports whether end-of-file has been encountered; ferror reports whether a stream error occurred. EOF is usually detected after a read attempt fails to produce another character.

Check all return values, object lifetimes, types and preconditions. Enable compiler warnings and test expected as well as failure paths.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: fgetc stores its result in int so EOF remains distinguishable from byte values. After the loop, ferror checks whether the read stopped because of an error.

practise.guidedTask: Why is int used for ch instead of char?
practise.independentTask: Read a text file character by character and report separately whether reading ended normally or failed.
hints: Check the read result first; then inspect ferror or feof when needed.
EOF is a macro value, not a character stored in the file.
Always close a stream after successful opening, including error paths.
